strengths: Novel and elegant Feynman diagram framework dramatically simplifying finite-width NTK calculations compared to direct algebraic approaches
Rigorous theoretical development with three main theorems establishing correctness and all-order extendability, supported by detailed proofs via diagram reconstruction

New theoretical results: extension of stability to finite-width NTK statistics, first derivation of NTK mean correction recursion, generalized proof of scale-invariance for arbitrary activation functions

Comprehensive experimental validation with excellent agreement to Monte Carlo samples (widths n ≳ 20), thorough stability analysis to 30 layers, systematic study across multiple activation functions and tensor types

Exceptional reproducibility: complete Feynman rule specifications, detailed implementation with tensor symmetry exploitation, all experimental parameters, 29-page appendices enabling independent verification
weaknesses: Limited scope: restricted to MLPs at initialization for leading-order 1/n corrections; no demonstration of extensibility to modern architectures or training dynamics
Unclear practical applicability: finite-width corrections useful only at modest widths (n ≳ 20-100) while modern networks are substantially wider; impact on practical machine learning unclear
Incremental advances on established frameworks: finite-width expansion from [16,17], stability analysis following from [18] rules, scale-invariance generalizing known ReLU results [38,39]
Extreme presentation density with heavy reliance on 29-page appendices; Feynman diagram notation requires significant parsing effort; limited pedagogical introduction to QFT connection
Experimental limitations: relatively small networks (max 300 width), only synthetic settings, validation primarily via Monte Carlo comparison, missing runtime/complexity analysis and ablation studies
Incomplete higher-order theory: Theorem 4.3 requires enumerating arbitrary rank tensors with unclear convergence properties at high orders; limited discussion of when 1/n expansion breaks down
